Date: 2026-06-18
Start: 15:30 UTC

Location: Zoom
Redwood host(s): Samir Patel, Leah Ortiz
Customer: Claremont Diagnostics (Priya, Evan, Marta, Jin)
Meeting type: Discovery - private/on-prem intake
summary: Initial intake for vaulted-network (air-gapped) private deployment. Customer is regulated diagnostics lab exploring Redwood Private in an isolated datacenter. Primary concerns: offline updates, hardware constraints, KMS integration and auditability. Action items include sharing security docs, hardware footprint, and scheduling a deeper infra lab test.
topics: KMS/HSM & key provisioning in isolated networks
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood, and with me is Leah our solutions engineer. before we dive can you confirm attendees?
[00:12] Priya: yeah hi this is Dr. Priya Menon, CTO at Claremont Diagnostics — with Evan infra lead, Marta compliance, and Jin ML. thanks for setting this up.
[00:20] Samir: perfect, thanks. quick agenda — understand your environment, constraints for a vaulted/offline deployment, security reqs, and next steps. sound good?
[00:32] Evan: yep, that's what we're after. we run a private datacenter here, network egress is effectively zero, everything is air-gapped. we want to host inference on-prem for regulatory reasons.
[00:44] Leah: ok great — can you walk me through the hardware you have on-prem? GPUs, racks, how you handle firmware updates?
[00:52] Evan: mainly older gen cards — some A100s but mostly 16GB-ish T4/RTX6000s, a few newer 80GB instances in a separate cluster. patch windows are monthly and very strict, any inbound packages need to go through our Change Control board.
[01:10] Leah: understood. from Redwood Private perspective we support pinned model versions and an update image you can airgap in — we commonly ship signed artifacts that can be brought in via approved media. quick note: some model quantization/optimizations require specific drivers or CUDA versions.
[01:27] Marta: signed artifacts are fine but our compliance team will need to validate signatures and verify checksums. also keys cannot leave the vault. we use an internal HSM and Vault (HashiCorp). how do you integrate KMS or HSM in a closed network?
[01:42] Samir: good question. we offer a customer-managed KMS integration — for private deployments we can either run a lightweight KMS proxy in the environment that talks only to your HSM, or use an offline key-init flow where keys are generated and stored locally. Leah, want to add the details on the offline key-init?
[01:58] Leah: sure — there are two patterns we recommend. 1) KMS proxy that sits in the VPC and is authorized to the HSM, all token encryption uses that same HSM; 2) fully air-gapped key import where the customer generates keys and we ship a signed binary that uses those keys locally. both patterns keep secrets in customer control.
[02:18] Jin: if we go with local keys, how does Redwood handle model updates and code signing? our CI/CD is external and we can't have a direct pull.
[02:26] Samir: you'd receive signed release artifacts and a manifest file. the manifest is signed by Redwood, you verify signatures against the public key we've exchanged. the update can be applied during your maintenance window. we also provide a verification script.
[02:39] Priya: is there a supported workflow for incremental model patching? we don't want to re-provision the entire node on every small security patch.
[02:47] Leah: yes — our runtime supports component-level updates: runtime, model blob, and policy config can be updated separately. small quantized weights can be rsynced via secure transfer medium. for larger model deltas we ship delta packages that apply in-place.
[03:05] Evan: ok that helps. second concern is auditability — we need detailed audit logs for every inference request for 12 months. can Redwood produce tokenized logs without exposing sensitive patient data?
[03:17] Samir: we support audit logging with PII redaction hooks. logs can be written to local storage or to your internal logging pipeline. we can also offer an on-device redaction lambda where the raw input never leaves the node and only metadata and permitted fields are stored.
[03:34] Marta: do you have SOC 2 / ISO attestation for this product? we need evidence for our auditor.
[03:41] Samir: yes — we have SOC2 Type II and ISO27001 for our hosted/control-plane components. for Private deployments we provide a compliance pack with architecture diagrams and the controls mapping. i'll send the security pack after this call.
[03:55] Priya: good. latency/cost question — our models are moderate in size (7B-ish) but with a 512-token context for some RN flows. we're targeting p95 under 400ms for short prompts. is that realistic on older cards?
[04:09] Leah: depends a lot on batching, kv cache, and quantization. on T4-ish hardware 7B quantized to 4-bit can be good for sub-second p95 with low batching; but for consistent 400ms p95 we'd recommend a newer 80GB runtime or multiple smaller replicas with warm KV caches. we can run a sample benchmark with your workload to give a realistic number.
[04:33] Jin: what about continuous batching — since we're in a closed network and can't rely on hosted pooling, do you support local request coalescing?
[04:40] Leah: yes — the runtime includes a local batching layer that aggregates requests on the node. in private deployments that runs as part of the inference service. you can configure max latency vs batch size tradeoffs.
[04:51] Evan: network segmentation question: we have an isolated rack with no outbound. can the control plane live in our DMZ?
[04:58] Samir: Reddit — sorry, Redwood's control plane usually remains in our cloud, but for fully disconnected deployments we offer a private control plane option that we can run as a managed instance in your environment or as a fully offline operator. for regulatory reasons some customers prefer a self-hosted control plane VM that only communicates on scheduled windows.
[05:18] Priya: scheduled windows are our preference — we can allow outbound to a management jumpbox for a one-hour window monthly. any tool that needs to phone home outside that schedule won't work.
[05:27] Leah: totally fine — we can do a pull model where signed manifests are pulled in during the allowed window. we also support a push model via USB transfer if needed. small note: telemetry and usage metrics won't be sent unless you opt in and configure a proxy.
[05:44] Marta: what's the support SLA for this Private setup? we need on-call during business hours and standby for critical incidents.
[05:51] Samir: for Private & Dedicated customers we offer enterprise support bundles, you can choose 8x5 or 24x7 with on-site escalation add-ons. there are also runbook handoffs and runbook-as-code we can template for your ops.
[06:05] Jin: model versioning — can we pin models per environment and do canary rollouts within the air-gapped cluster?
[06:12] Leah: yes, the rollout controller supports canary within an internal subnet. because there's no external telemetry, rollouts depend on local health checks and metrics you configure. we also have a percent-based rollout that can be configured by node label.
[06:27] Evan: would we be able to fallback to a smaller model if memory pressure spikes?
[06:31] Leah: we support automatic fallback policies to a compatible, lower-memory model variant. memory pressure thresholds can trigger fallback or queueing. fallback requires the fallback model to be present on disk or in cache; we recommend pre-staging small variants.
[06:44] Priya: security question — do you support SAML/Okta for RBAC into the management console? our SSO must be enforced.
[06:52] Samir: yes SSO via SAML/OIDC is supported. for completely offline control planes we integrate with your internal IdP via SAML metadata exchange or local LDAP/AD.
[07:02] Marta: what about encryption at rest for model blobs and intermediate KV cache?
[07:07] Leah: model blobs are encrypted at rest using customer-managed keys (if provided), and KV cache can be encrypted using dm-crypt or equivalent. we also maintain a cryptographic checksum manifest to detect tampering.
[07:20] Evan: one operational question: how are model artifacts stored on disk? we have limited SSD capacity and would prefer not to store multiple full model copies.
[07:28] Leah: the runtime uses a layered storage approach: model shards can be memory-mapped and you can set eviction policies for cold replicas. we support storing deltas to reduce disk overhead. for multiple models we often recommend a cache-tier SSD + slower archival store.
[07:44] Jin: can you run vector embeddings and a small reranker locally as part of the same pipeline?
[07:50] Samir: yep — embeddings and reranker modules can run colocated. many customers run an on-node embedding index and a small reranker to avoid outbound calls.
[07:59] Priya: compliance needs — do you provide a template for the auditor showing separation of duties and audit controls?
[08:06] Samir: yes, that's part of the compliance pack I'll send: roles, responsibilities, network diagram, and evidence mapping.
[08:14] Evan: about hardware — if we wanted performance similar to your hosted lowest-latency profile, what would you recommend?
[08:21] Leah: likely an 80GB HBM card (like an A100 80GB or equivalent) with NVIDIA driver 535+ and CUDA 12.x for best perf on 7B+ on 512 token sequences. if budget's tight, two smaller cards with sharding can work but adds complexity.
[08:38] Priya: budgeting concerns — what's the delta between Dedicated reserved vs Private (air-gapped) setup in terms of ops/setup cost?
[08:45] Samir: Dedicated reserved is simpler: we operate infra and you get SLA on throughput. Private has higher one-time onboarding (deploying control plane, integrating with HSM, runbook), plus optional premium support. i'll follow up with a cost matrix.
[08:59] Jin: for the benchmark, what do you need from us?
[09:02] Leah: an anonymized request corpus (like 200 sample requests), target qps and p95 target, model size, and maximum acceptable cold-start time. we'll run a lab on similar hardware and send results.
[09:16] Priya: can the lab use our models or do you require a protobuf?
[09:20] Leah: we can run both. preferred is an anonymized model or a functionally identical small model. we also accept a serialized checkpoint if you can provide it under an NDA.
[09:34] Evan: let's talk about maintenance windows — are there recommended cadence and rollback procedures?
[09:39] Leah: recommended cadence often mirrors OS patches: monthly for critical patches, quarterly for model upgrades. rollback uses atomic change sets; we store previous manifests so you can revert to the prior pinned version quickly.
[09:51] Marta: are there known gotchas for customers with very limited outbound? we've seen things like driver mismatches during updates.
[09:59] Leah: drivers and CUDA are the usual friction points. we always test the runtime on your pinned driver versions in our lab. also GPU firmware updates may require coordination with hardware vendors—we can include that in the runbook.
[10:13] Samir: quick check — any blockers from your side right now for starting a pilot?
[10:19] Priya: timeline: we need procurement signoff and an internal security review. target is a pilot in Q3.our auditor needs the compliance pack before procurement greenlight.
[10:30] Samir: understood. we'll get the compliance pack and a draft SOW to you.
[10:35] Jin: small technical question: does Redwood runtime support mixed precision quantization for faster perf? and can that be done offline?
[10:44] Leah: yes, mixed-precision and q4/q2 variants are supported. quantization profiles can be generated from a small calibration corpus and applied offline — the artifacts can be transferred into the air-gapped environment.
[10:58] Evan: curious about observability — how do we surface per-route latency and cost internally without sending data out?
[11:07] Samir: we have a local observability stack option: Prometheus metrics, local traces, and a UI that runs in your network. metrics are stored locally and can be rolled up to your internal monitoring.
[11:19] Marta: do you provide a guidance doc for least-privilege roles for ops?
[11:24] Leah: yes — the role templates are in the compliance pack and include runbook permissions and suggested RBAC policies.
[11:33] Priya: great. anything else on security?
[11:36] Marta: one more — we require periodic key rotation that we manage. is rotation supported without downtime?
[11:42] Leah: supported — we provide key-rotation tooling that can perform in-place rotation with dual-key acceptance window to avoid downtime. rotation requires coordination but is doable.
[11:55] Samir: we should capture specific next steps — i'll send the compliance and SOC2/ISO pack, Leah will draft the hardware footprint and benchmark plan, Jin will share sample requests.
[12:07] Priya: noted. also please include a short checklist for the Change Control Board so we can present it.
[12:13] Samir: yes, checklist will be included.
[12:17] Evan: curious on fallback — if we lose a node mid-inference, how are partial results handled?
[12:24] Leah: inference is mostly atomic per request; we checkpoint KV cache periodically and incomplete requests either fail-fast or re-queue depending on your policy. we can tune retries.
[12:36] Jin: do you support model sharding across multiple GPUs when single model doesn't fit on one card?
[12:42] Leah: yes, tensor/model-parallel sharding is supported but requires newer drivers and orchestration; we typically recommend 80GB cards to avoid it, but we can enable sharding if needed.
[12:56] Priya: let's talk timeline again — pilot in Q3 would be ideal. procurement needs a cost-scenario: minimal viable pilot (single rack) vs full production.
[13:07] Samir: we'll include a two-tier pricing scenario: pilot (one node cluster + support) and production (multi-node + premium support + runbook services).
[13:18] Marta: please also call out the onetime integration labor estimate for HSM and SSO.
[13:23] Samir: will do.
[13:27] Evan: about backups — do we keep model artifacts offsite?
[13:31] Leah: backup is fully customer controlled. we recommend a local air-gapped archive or encrypted tape, per your policy.
[13:40] Jin: for the benchmark dataset, any size limits?
[13:44] Leah: 200-500 representative requests is usually enough. also include distribution of short vs long prompts.
[13:52] Samir: quick note — I'll drop links in the follow-up: compliance pack (https://redwood.company/secure-deploy-pack.pdf), benchmark template (drive/benchmark-claremont.xlsx), and a proposed SOW draft.
[14:09] Priya: thanks. one more operational question: can we opt to run Redwood runtime inside an air-gapped Kubernetes cluster or do you prefer systemd-managed services?
[14:18] Leah: both. many customers run it as a K8s daemonset for easier orchestrations; others prefer bare-metal systemd services for stricter isolation. we'll provide best-practice manifests.
[14:30] Evan: manifest templates would help.
[14:33] Samir: final quick recap then we'll open for any last questions. recap: send compliance/SOC2 pack, hardware footprint, benchmark plan, sample data, scheduling of tech deep-dive. target pilot Q3.
[14:48] Jin: sounds good.
[14:51] Marta: thanks everyone.
[14:55] Samir: thanks all. we'll follow up in email; expect docs by end of this week.
[15:00] Priya: bye.
[15:02] Leah: bye.

Notes: transcription has minor errors - some names or acronyms may be lightly mangled. Linked artifacts referenced: https://redwood.company/secure-deploy-pack.pdf, drive/benchmark-claremont.xlsx (internal), sample SOW draft (attached in follow-up).
